title: The Trump team’s troublesome tech outages response | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Two weeks after the GOP’s shellacking in the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration is embroiled in a crisis that it has often made worse with its messaging.

A series of tech outages impacting air travel, banks, online communications and even a highly classified network used by the National Security Agency has Americansspooked — and often wondering what’s going on.

And the messaging from the administration has been so confusing — or, in some cases, largely absent — that it’s fed into the growing unease.

It’s gotten to the point where former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt on Tuesday took to pointing out when members of the administrationactually getit right, in her estimation.

Former Trump Homeland Security spokeswoman Tricia McLaughlin added on X: “Americans aren’t stupid.We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.”

Here’s a look at how some of the main players — including some who could succeed Trump as the GOP presidential standard-bearer — have handled things.

President Donald Trump is now telling Americans concerned about the tech outages to “relax.”

“Tell them to relax. Everything’s good. These are individual events,” the president told Fox News in an interview in China that aired Wednesday night.

Largely, his problem has been his absence — his lack of any public presence on the issue and his lack of reassurance in a scary time.

He said virtually nothing for two days about Friday’s rare and chaotic full ground stop at the nation’s airports, even as he posted repeatedly on social media about renovation projects like Washington’s public golf course. By Sunday, he posted blaming the Biden administration and asking Congress for more money to modernize the Federal Aviation Administration.

By Monday, he said hedidn’t “take any responsibility”for the ground stop. He said he had been working in the Oval Office when it happened but had delegated the messaging to others.

“I didn’t think there was any reason for me to do (it),” Trump told reporters while departing the White House for Asia.

And his comments are making him look increasingly out of touch. Before telling Americans to relax about the tech outages, he effectively shrugged them off.

“It’s life,” Trump said after landing in the Philippines when asked whether he was concerned about the outages. “When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

One of the main lessons of the 2026 election was that voters saw Trump as unconcerned about their priorities. His response to these outageshas been a case in point.

Trump has never been good at empathizing. But he doesn’t even seem to be trying.

Perhaps nobody has come in for criticismlike Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Even MAGA-aligned conservative commentators have called him “a buffoon” and “unfit for office,” with Megyn Kelly saying she has “zero faith in this man.”

The reason has been a characteristically unsteady stream of messages, compounded with a highly questionable decision tofly to a college football gameon Saturday, even as many Americans were still stranded. (Mullin has stressed that he’s required to fly in a government plane because of his job.)

Mullin kicked things off Friday amid the ground stop by saying that he didn’t “want to say this is a crisis, but it is.” He then began Friday night’s press conference with a pretty tone-deaf joke about how it was Friday the 13th. (There are few people with less of a sense of humor than the stranded traveler.)

By Monday, he was offering speculation about what was happening with the tech outages based on “one guy that’s very smart with tech” but was “not Elon (Musk).” It was a performance more befitting of a TV pundit than the guy in charge of responding to the crisis.

But Mullin’s biggest optics problem was deciding to go to the Texas-LSU football game on Saturday, which was first reported Tuesday morning by the New York Post. When challenged about that decision Tuesday on CNBC, Mullin noted that the airspace at the time was “completely open” — although many people were still stranded — and said that even as he’s working hard, “we’ve still got to live our life at the same time.”

Talk about tone-deaf.

Mullin kept trying to explain at a congressional hearing Wednesday, telling the House Homeland Security Committee that canceling his travel plans would have looked like “distrust that we’re not even willing to fly.” But that sounds quite different from his initial explanation. And it seems a little too cute by half.

The thing is, to those familiar with Mullin’s TV appearances even before he became DHS secretary, he’s always had this in him. The former Oklahoma senator gets things wrong. He’s often off-message. It’s just that this is the first time it’s been front and center for the American public. And he compounded that with aTed Cruz-leveltravel gaffe.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s problem has been his choice of message — basically blaming the ground stop on a lack of FAA modernization funding from Congress.

The first problem is that he previously scoffed at this kind of blame-shifting. AsCNN’s Andrew Kaczynski reports, after a 2023 ground stop under the Biden administration, Duffy suggested the problem was leadership rather than funding.

“They got billions of dollars, the FAA did, over Covid,” Duffysaid on Fox Newsat the time. “And now they’re gonna come back and say, ‘We want even more money to fix this crisis that we weren’t able to handle when, you know, for what, three hours in the morning aircraft couldn’t, couldn’t fly.’”

The second is that while Duffy has been consistently asking for more money, he’s rubbed even Republicans the wrong way with his latest request.

After previously asking for $30 billion more for FAA modernization, he quickly jacked that up to $50 billion — but without saying why. Congressional Republicans have balked both at theimplication that they were to blamefor what happened Friday and at the idea that they shouldjust shovel money on topof the $12.5 billion that Congress approved in the GOP’s spending and policy bill last year, when that hasn’t all been marked as spent yet.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has increasingly been dispatched — including at Wednesday’s hearing — in an apparent effort to steady the ship.

During aFox Business appearanceTuesday and at Wednesday’s hearing, he’s sought to underscore the administration’s conclusion that the tech outages aren’t due to some malign foreign actor.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said at the hearing. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”

It was pretty standard stuff from the administration, but it was delivered with the kind of confidence and authority that has been lacking elsewhere.

Leavitt on Tuesdaypraised the decision to dispatch Clayton— the implication being that he was an improvement on the others.

Leavitt has alsoconspicuously praisedSecretary of State Marco Rubio, who has stepped forward to offer the empathy and concern that Trump hasn’t.

Rubio acknowledged while in the Philippines this week that the outages highlight important questions about “vulnerabilities” in our technology. He also nodded to people being “nervous” and “anxious.”

He added at another point: “We fully acknowledge that this is unsettling, to see these reports, day after day, of some technical failures. … We get it.”

“We take these things very seriously,” Rubio added. “Obviously, we’re always vigilant.”

Again, standard leader stuff. But it underscored the lack of similar comments from Trump.

Vice President JD Vance hasn’t said as much as other players, but he did make some pretty big news Wednesday by abruptly canceling his appearance at the New York Times’ DealBook Summit. The stated reason: He was asked to attend meetings in Washington amid the tech outages.

It’s unclear what (or who) specifically prompted the last-minute cancellation. Vance has clearly been trying to craft a brand somewhat independent of Trump. And Wednesday’s was an interesting move, given the president’s lack of public attention to the issue and that fact that some have questioned whether he should have canceled his own plans to travel to Asia.

Vance has also wandered into some trouble, though. After he echoed the party line of blaming the administration’s predecessors for the state of the nation’s air travel system, even Fox News’ Laura Ingraham balked.

“Well, you guys have been in charge the last two years,” Ingrahaminterjected, adding: “Why hasn’t it gotten fixed?”

The entire episode has also underscored the strange lack of a replacement for Leavitt.

It’s been nearly three months since she left her job in late August. It’s also been almost a month since her initial replacement, Katie Zacharia, was fired after just five days.

These are moments when the administration could really use disciplined messengers fully devoted to briefing the media every day. But apparently they can’t find the right person — and those filling the void have struggled.
